solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: While singer goes around hotel, it’s disgusting

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: an alto is a singer with a low female or high male voice
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the exclamation you make at something disgusting

explanation.surface: Someone is revolted while a singer wanders round a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'While' looks like a time word opening the scene, but it is the definition in its concessive sense: ALT(H)O + UGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are conjunctions conceding a point, as in 'while I agree' meaning 'though I agree'.

clue.text: Granted, nothing has yet been settled?

blocks.note: granted as in permitted
if no debt is settled, every penny is still owing; read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is cryptic, flagged by the question mark: split the answer as ALL OWED and it describes a bill with nothing yet paid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something granted has been permitted; the split reading describes unpaid debts in full.

clue.text: Crossing path with one going around states

indicators.note: something going is leaving, so a letter departs from the word it sat in
to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a path is a TRAIL, which contains I (one); that I departs
to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A path runs across while someone walks round the states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With one going' reads as company on the walk; it means the path loses its I (one), and 'states' is the verb, not the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A traversal is a passage across something, the act of going from one side to the other.

clue.text: Part of a general misery in old town? Not half

indicators.note: only half survives, so the word loses its second half
one thing placed within another sits inside it

blocks.note: hell is utter misery
O is a standard abbreviation for old
only the first half of TOWN is kept

explanation.surface: An old soldier's misery in an old town, told with a shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello is Shakespeare's Moorish general, so the 'part' is a stage role; 'Not half' keeps just the front of the town.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is the title role in Shakespeare's tragedy, a character who commands Venetian armies as a general.

clue.text: Blunder installing extremely inferior browser

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters count
installing something puts it inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: a gaffe is a social blunder
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A tech mistake: someone installs a truly bad web browser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browser' reads as software; here it is an animal that browses, feeding on leaves high in trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A browser is any animal that grazes on shoots and leaves, and the tall African herbivore is the classic example.

clue.text: Group with intelligence probing what follows fa or do

indicators.note: a probe pushes inside something, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: in do-re-mi-fa-sol, the note after fa
the US Central Intelligence Agency

explanation.surface: A music lesson: which note follows fa, or do?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like another sol-fa note beside fa, but it is the definition: a do is a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British words for a party or gathering where people meet and mingle.

clue.text: Sauces from Italy served up and desirable sweet food

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: ragu is an Italian meat sauce
a plum job is a desirable one

explanation.surface: An Italian meal: sauces are served, and then something sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: Plum as an adjective means choice or much sought after, as in a plum role.
explanation.definitionFit: A sugarplum is a small round sweet or candied confection, the kind dancing in Christmas stories.

clue.text: Stun people who are inside entertaining clubs with cruciverbalists

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds others

blocks.note: convicts, who are inside prison
C for clubs, the card suit
the setter and solvers, crossword people, are us

explanation.surface: Prisoners laying on a card night for crossword fans, and knocking them out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' is British slang for in prison, and cruciverbalists, crossword people, means the setter and solvers themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: To concuss someone is to knock them senseless with a blow, a medical sense of stun.

clue.text: Set hammered gold on dresses without any frills

indicators.note: hammered metal is beaten out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order
to dress something is to clothe it, so an outer piece wraps an inner one

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
the anagram fodder
re means on or about, as in a memo

explanation.surface: A jeweller sets hammered gold on plain, unfussy dresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresses' looks like clothing in the surface; it is a verb, with AU and RE wrapping the jumbled SET.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere describes something plain and severe, lacking decoration or comfort, stripped to essentials.

clue.text: Striking German cycle on grassy area

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: a lea is a meadow
Wagner's Ring cycle, Der Ring des Nibelungen

explanation.surface: A German cycling over a meadow, striking in appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German cycle' suggests a bicycle; it is Wagner's four-opera Ring cycle. 'On' in an across clue puts the ring after LEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Leathering is British slang for beating someone, originally thrashing with a leather strap.

clue.text: Some scoff “I won’t pipe down”

blocks.note: a flat refusal
the call for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at an order to keep quiet and refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' looks like a verb of mockery; it is British slang for food. Told 'Sh!', the rebel answers 'No!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoff and nosh are both informal British words for food, so some scoff is a snack.

clue.text: Feel how criminal gets riches and fateful revolver

indicators.note: something criminal is bent, so the letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder
a fortune is great wealth

explanation.surface: A thief gets rich, and a gun decides someone's fate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' suggests a gun; it is anything that turns, here the wheel that the goddess Fortune spins.
explanation.definitionFit: The wheel of fortune is the spinning wheel of fate from medieval allegory, deciding luck by turning.

clue.text: Beginning to strip, rip off long clothes?

definitions.text: Beginning to strip, rip off long clothes?

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the opening letter counts
to clothe something is to cover it, so one piece wraps others

blocks.note: to be dying for something is to long for it
its first letter
to rip someone off is to rob them

explanation.surface: Someone starts a striptease, ripping off long garments.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: every word builds letters, and the full sentence also describes undressing. Long means to be dying for something.
explanation.definitionFit: To disrobe is to take off your clothes, exactly what starting to strip and ripping off garments involves.

clue.text: The sticks supporter placed around Buddhist temple

indicators.note: something placed around another surrounds it on all sides

blocks.note: a backer is a financial supporter
a wat is a Buddhist temple in Thailand or Cambodia

explanation.surface: A patron builds a fence of sticks round a Buddhist temple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The sticks' reads as bits of wood; it is the idiom for remote countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: The sticks is an idiom for a remote rural place, and a backwater is an isolated, sleepy place.

clue.text: Column but not newspaper’s cover

indicators.note: something kept but not something else means that item is left out

blocks.note: a pilaster is a flat column set into a wall
the i is a British national newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper column that fails to make the front page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' and 'newspaper' look like journalism; the column is architectural, and the newspaper is the i, a British daily, whose letter comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: To plaster a surface is to coat it thickly, as with plaster on a wall, a synonym of cover.

clue.text: Item worn when eg, running dog gets fit

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow or track them
to suit is to fit, as clothes suit you

explanation.surface: A running dog gets fit, and something is worn for jogging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running dog' reads as one picture; the comma after eg ends the definition, and dog is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracksuit is the loose top and trousers athletes wear when training, such as for a jog.

clue.text: Gag, as cracked by the French

indicators.note: something cracked open has another thing forced into it

blocks.note: as and since both mean because
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A joke that the French crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' reads as a joke, fitting the cracking; it is the verb for muzzling someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To gag someone is to stop them speaking, which is to silence them.

clue.text: Providing gospel, I will need two parts of the Bible

definitions.note: a phrase that gives gospel truth, used adverbially like the answer

blocks.note: carried straight through
NT, the New Testament, and Ruth, a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A preacher says that to deliver the gospel they need two sections of scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible theme runs through the surface, and 'gospel' belongs to it; it is also the gospel truth that the answer phrase delivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking gospel means stating something utterly true, which is saying it honestly, really, indeed.

clue.text: Starter of Chinese leaves in pastry whilst travelling

indicators.note: the starter of a meal comes first, so only the opening letter counts
something that leaves goes away, so it drops out of the word

blocks.note: its first letter
en croute is the French culinary term for baked in a pastry crust

explanation.surface: A Chinese starter, with leaves in pastry, eaten on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinese leaves' is a vegetable in the surface, but leaves is the verb: the C departs from EN CROUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: En route is borrowed French for on the way, which is what a person travelling is.

clue.text: Charge £0.01 per person to cross motorway

indicators.note: a thing lying across another straddles it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: one penny, written 1p, with the digit read as the letter I
a price per person is so much each
British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on

explanation.surface: A toll: a penny per head to use the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like a price, supporting the toll picture; it means accuse. The 1 of 1p becomes I.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach an official is to formally accuse them of wrongdoing, a legal sense of charge.

clue.text: Reluctance to move home? It’s overturned, in time

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped upside down, so in a down clue its letters run backwards
one thing placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: at home is in
the word as printed; the apostrophe-s that follows is just 'is'
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone hates moving house, and the house has been turned upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reluctance to move home?' reads as one phrase; the definition stops at move, and home gives IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is the tendency to stay put and resist change, in physics and in lazy human habit.

clue.text: Dashed hope upset proof-reader for The Sun?

indicators.note: dashed hopes are smashed, so the letters are broken into a new order
something upset is knocked over, so in a down clue it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: the anagram fodder
a sub-editor checks copy for errors

explanation.surface: A subeditor at The Sun tabloid, hopes crushed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid, so 'proof-reader for The Sun' reads as a newspaper job; the question mark flags the sun itself, personified as a god.
explanation.definitionFit: Phoebus, meaning bright one, is an epithet of Apollo as Greek god of the sun, and poetic for it.

clue.text: One hoping for a lift from big song, say, by pop singer

blocks.note: a chart-topping record, say is its example marker
the American singer Cher

explanation.surface: Someone hopes a big pop song will lift their mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lift from a big song' reads as a mood boost; the lift is a free ride, and 'by' simply puts CHER beside HIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitcher, or hitchhiker, thumbs the roadside hoping a driver will offer a free ride.

clue.text: Puzzle which involves energy, caution and discipline

indicators.note: something that involves others takes them in, so it holds pieces inside

blocks.note: to throw someone is to baffle them
which and that are both relative pronouns
E is the symbol for energy
a referee books a player to caution them

explanation.surface: A puzzle that takes energy, care and self-control.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface praises a crossword; each word then gets a second sense. In football, booking a player is formally cautioning them.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw the book at someone is an idiom for punishing them as severely as the rules allow.

clue.text: African place to spend a penny whilst seeing wild animals, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the words count for their sound, not their spelling

blocks.clueFragment: place to spend a penny whilst seeing wild animals
blocks.note: a loo is a toilet, and spend a penny is British for using one; the animals are at a zoo

explanation.surface: Needing the toilet on a safari trip, or so we're told.
explanation.walkthrough: A zoo's toilet would be a zoo loo. 'African' reads as a safari setting; it is the definition, for a member of the southern African people.
explanation.definitionFit: The Zulu are a Bantu people of South Africa, so a Zulu is an African person.

clue.text: Item for cleaning excessively black bird cages

indicators.note: to cage something is to shut it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: too much is excessively
a common songbird
B for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Scrubbing a bird's cage that has turned filthy black.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a bird in a cage; the wordplay turns it round so the bird does the caging, closing round black.
explanation.definitionFit: A toothbrush is the small brush used daily for scrubbing teeth, a household cleaning tool.

clue.text: How terrible daughter blocks catch with ball, at first

indicators.note: something that blocks a passage sits in the middle of it
placed at the start, so this piece leads the rest

blocks.note: a ball is round, like the letter O
to catch what someone says is to hear it
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A cricket disaster: a daughter fumbles a catch with the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' and 'ball' suggest cricket; catch means hear, and the O leads.
explanation.definitionFit: Oh dear is the mild exclamation of dismay said when something unfortunate happens.

clue.text: Strength drug swallowed by Mr Muscle

indicators.note: something swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a strength is an asset
E is ecstasy
carried straight through

explanation.surface: A bodybuilder called Mr Muscle swallows a strength drug.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Muscle reads as one name, a British cleaning brand; it splits so that Muscle is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The masseter is the thick jaw muscle that closes the mouth, working hard in chewing.
